evidence.claim: The Cohutta-Chattahoochee Scenic Byway crosses rolling farmland before climbing into the Cohutta Mountains.
evidence.quote: follows State Route 2 past rolling pastoral lands into Murray County. Breathtaking views of the Cohutta Mountains emerge

evidence.claim: Georgia DOT includes it among the state’s designated scenic byways, describing a 54-mile route linking pastoral land, national forest and a mountaintop overlook.
evidence.quote: The 54-mile route skirts the town of Chatsworth before traveling up State Route 52, passing Fort Mountain State Park and ending at a beautiful mountaintop overlook.

evidence.claim: Georgia DOT includes it among the state’s designated scenic byways
evidence.quote: corridors that have achieved Georgia Scenic Byways status as designated by the Georgia DOT.

evidence.claim: On Fort Mountain, State Route 52 is steep and curving, with views of the Cohutta Mountains and an overlook with parking.
evidence.quote: A steep, curving scenic route, Georgia SR 52, runs east-west between Chatsworth and Ellijay, affording views of the Cohutta Mountains; there is at least one overlook with parking.

evidence.claim: The climb east of Chatsworth takes SR 2 and SR 52 from around 800 feet to above 2,500 feet before the roads curve southeast.
evidence.quote: The routes climb from around 800 feet elevation to above 2,500 feet, before curving to the southeast

evidence.claim: The mountain highway acquired its present number in stages.
evidence.quote: It was then just one more year before the portion of the route between Dalton and Ellijay was re-designated as SR 52

evidence.claim: The Dalton-to-Chatsworth section had already appeared on state road maps in 1920 as part of SR 2.
evidence.quote: The first portion of the roadway that is signed as SR 52 today makes its appearance on Georgia state road maps in 1920, when the 13.4 miles (21.6 km) portion of the current route from its western terminus to Chatsworth, which is concurrent with US 76, was already in existence, and signed as part of SR2.

evidence.claim: By early 1932, a new road section connected Chatsworth with Ellijay under the SR 2 designation.
evidence.quote: By the beginning of 1932, the western portion of the route was extended to now feature a new 22.6 miles (36.4 km) section from Chatsworth to Ellijay, also signed as SR 2.

evidence.claim: The Dalton-to-Ellijay stretch became SR 52 in 1949, completing that highway’s routing and designation.
evidence.quote: The remaining gaps in the route were closed in 1948

evidence.claim: The Dalton-to-Ellijay stretch became SR 52 in 1949, completing that highway’s routing and designation.
evidence.quote: It was then just one more year before the portion of the route between Dalton and Ellijay was re-designated as SR 52, completing the routing and designation of this state highway.

evidence.claim: That numbered highway is one part of the scenic route, which also uses county roads.
evidence.quote: the route continues along US 41 and quiet county roads into the Chattahoochee National Forest.

evidence.claim: Begin at Prater’s Mill in Whitfield County and follow SR 2 through the rolling land into Murray County.
evidence.quote: Beginning at historic Prater's Mill in Whitfield County, the Cohutta-Chattahoochee Scenic Byway follows State Route 2 past rolling pastoral lands into Murray County.

evidence.claim: The byway continues into the Chattahoochee National Forest, skirts Chatsworth and climbs SR 52 past Fort Mountain State Park to its final overlook.
evidence.quote: The 54-mile route skirts the town of Chatsworth before traveling up State Route 52, passing Fort Mountain State Park and ending at a beautiful mountaintop overlook.

evidence.claim: Spurs lead to the Cohutta Fish Hatchery and a Forest Service campsite along Holly Creek.
evidence.quote: Spurs off the route take visitors to the Cohutta Fish Hatchery and to a Forest Service camp site along Holly Creek.

evidence.claim: SR 52’s mountain stretch has views of the Cohutta Mountains and an overlook with parking.
evidence.quote: affording views of the Cohutta Mountains; there is at least one overlook with parking.

evidence.claim: A turbine beneath the water does the work at Prater’s Mill.
evidence.quote: The turbine is situated at the bottom of a 9-ft. deep pool called a forebay.

evidence.claim: Water enters a nine-foot-deep forebay, then rushes through gates to spin the turbine’s vanes and shaft.
evidence.quote: As the gates open, water from the forebay rushes into the turbine, spinning its vanes and turning the turbine shaft.

evidence.claim: John Pitner built the gristmill, sawmill and miller’s house in 1855.
evidence.quote: In 1855, pioneer businessman John Pitner built the grist mill, a sawmill and the miller’s house.

evidence.claim: His son-in-law Benjamin Franklin Prater inherited the site and expanded it into a complex with a blacksmith shop, country store, cotton gin and workers’ housing.
evidence.quote: his son-in-law Benjamin Franklin Prater inherited the site and led the development of a family-owned integrated mill complex including a blacksmith shop, country store, cotton gin and housing for workers.

evidence.claim: Customers could have horses shod and cotton ginned while their grain was processed.
evidence.quote: they could have their cotton ginned and horses shod while waiting for their grain to be processed.

evidence.claim: In the 1890s, Prater’s son William installed a flour-milling system, adding another service to the family operation.
evidence.quote: In the 1890s, Ben’s son William “Bill” Howard Prater installed a flour milling system in the grist mill

evidence.claim: Chatsworth began as a Louisville and Nashville Railroad depot in 1905.
evidence.quote: Chatsworth was founded in 1905 as a depot on the Louisville and Nashville Railroad.

evidence.claim: It became a town the following year, then took over as Murray County’s seat from Spring Place in 1915.
evidence.quote: It was incorporated as a town in 1906 and as a city in 1923. In 1915, the seat of Murray County transferred to Chatsworth from Spring Place

evidence.claim: The town sits west of Holly Creek’s valley, with Fort Mountain and Cohutta Mountain rising to the east.
evidence.quote: on the west side of the valley of Holly Creek, with 2,840-foot (870 m) Fort Mountain and 2,780-foot (850 m) Cohutta Mountain rising over the valley to the east.

evidence.claim: From here, SR 2 and SR 52 climb together into the Cohutta Mountains, passing Fort Mountain State Park seven miles east of the city center.
evidence.quote: Georgia State Routes 2 and 52 run together out of Chatsworth to the east, climbing into the Cohutta Mountains and passing through Fort Mountain State Park 7 miles (11 km) east of the city center.

evidence.claim: Holly Creek runs along the city’s eastern edge before joining the Conasauga River, part of the Oostanaula, Coosa and Alabama watershed.
evidence.quote: Holly Creek, which runs along the eastern edge of the city, is a south- and west-flowing tributary of the Conasauga River, part of the Oostanaula/Coosa/Alabama River watershed.

evidence.claim: Two stone structures share Fort Mountain’s highest ground: an ancient wall and a Civilian Conservation Corps fire tower.
evidence.quote: Hikers can also explore a stone fire tower built by the Civilian Conservation Corps and an ancient rock wall which stand on the highest point of the mountain.

evidence.claim: The wall zigzags across the summit, built from local stone.
evidence.quote: The zigzag wall contains 19 or 29 pits scattered along the wall, in addition to a ruin of a gateway. The wall was constructed out of local stones from the surrounding regions around the summit.

evidence.claim: A 1956 archaeological report called it a prehistoric construction but declined to assign a precise age or purpose without further investigation.
evidence.quote: represents a prehistoric aboriginal construction whose precise age and nature cannot yet be safely hazarded until the whole problem, of which this is a representative, has been more fully investigated.

evidence.claim: A 1956 archaeological report called it a prehistoric construction
evidence.quote: A 1956 archaeological report concluded only that the structure "represents a prehistoric aboriginal construction

evidence.claim: The CCC’s work extended beyond the tower to the lake, trails and park buildings.
evidence.quote: The Civilian Conservation Corps built many of the park's facilities, such as the stone fire tower, the lake, the trails and some park buildings.

evidence.claim: Trails wind through hardwood forest and blueberry thickets, cross streams and circle the lake.
evidence.quote: winding through hardwood forest and blueberry thickets, crossing streams and circling a pretty lake.

evidence.claim: The park occupies the southwestern end of the Cohutta Mountains, near the Cohutta Wilderness.
evidence.quote: Fort Mountain State Park sits at the southwestern end of the Cohutta Mountains near the Cohutta Wilderness.
